# Inference-Compute Budget vs. Attack Step Completion: Replication Across Model Families

**Problem:** The AISI 2026 finding that performance scales log-linearly with inference-time compute (10M→100M tokens yields up to 59% gains) has only been documented on a narrow set of frontier models. It is unknown whether this scaling law holds for open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen families).

**Direction:** Replicate the AISI inference-token budget experiment using open-weight models on a simplified 5-10 step cyber range (e.g., a local CTF-style Metasploitable VM chain). Vary token budget from 1K to 500K across model families and plot steps completed vs. log(tokens). Test whether log-linear scaling is a universal phenomenon or specific to frontier closed models.

**Why it matters:** If log-linear scaling is universal, even cheap open-weight models become significantly more dangerous with increased inference budget. If it is not, this tells evaluators which model families pose greater scaling risk. Directly addresses the lack of longitudinal cross-model comparison methodology.

**Relevant context:** Folkerts et al. 2026 (AISI) found log-linear scaling with no plateau: steps completed rose from 1.7 (GPT-4o) to 9.8 (Opus 4.6) over 18 months at fixed 10M token budget. At 100M tokens, Opus 4.6 averaged 1.4/7 ICS steps. The study covered only 7 frontier models. Open-weight replication would extend findings. (arxiv.org/abs/2603.11214)

# Copilot vs. Autonomous: Measuring the Amplification Factor in Guided Cyber Attack Scenarios

**Problem:** MITRE OCCULT identifies the human-AI copilot paradigm as the most realistic near-term threat but the least studied. Almost all existing evaluations measure fully autonomous AI performance. We have no data quantifying how much a human operator amplifies AI performance on multi-step tasks.

**Direction:** Design a controlled study where CS students with no security background (1) attempt a 5-step CTF-style challenge alone, (2) use an LLM autonomously, and (3) use an LLM in copilot mode (human provides high-level decisions, AI executes). Measure steps completed, time, and errors in each condition. Compute a 'copilot amplification factor'.

**Why it matters:** The copilot threat model is most relevant for real attackers yet least benchmarked. Measuring amplification quantitatively would directly fill the gap identified by OCCULT and inform policy thresholds: is a novice + AI equivalent to an expert alone?

title: CTF Difficulty Calibration Using Item Response Theory: Building a Principled Cyber Capability Scale

original_idea.body:
# CTF Difficulty Calibration Using Item Response Theory: Building a Principled Cyber Capability Scale

**Problem:** CTF benchmarks report raw solve rates (e.g., Cybench 82%) without calibrating item difficulty. A 50% solve rate on a hard challenge and a 50% rate on an easy challenge tell us different things about capability, but existing benchmarks treat them identically.

**Direction:** Apply 2-parameter IRT (difficulty + discrimination) to an existing CTF dataset (e.g., Cybench, NYU CTF Bench) using model solve/fail data across multiple models as 'examinees'. Fit IRT curves, estimate per-challenge difficulty and discrimination parameters, and generate a capability theta score for each model. Validate by checking if theta scores correlate with known model rankings.

**Why it matters:** IRT produces a principled, scale-invariant capability metric unaffected by benchmark difficulty distribution shifts, addressing the saturation problem (Cybench went 10%→82% making raw scores meaningless) and providing a foundation for longitudinal comparison.

**Relevant context:** Cambridge/Trismik applied IRT to AI evaluation (enterprise.cam.ac.uk). Cybench reached 93% saturation (CAIBench meta-benchmark, arxiv.org/html/2510.24317v1). AISI noted that no standardized longitudinal comparison methodology exists. IRT has been validated for LLM benchmarking in NLP contexts.

title: Mutation Testing for Cyber Benchmarks: Measuring Robustness of AI Performance to Challenge Perturbations

original_idea.body:
# Mutation Testing for Cyber Benchmarks: Measuring Robustness of AI Performance to Challenge Perturbations

**Problem:** AI models may be solving CTF challenges through memorization of training data rather than genuine reasoning. If a model has seen a challenge during training, solve rates are inflated. No systematic methodology exists to detect this contamination in cyber benchmarks.

**Direction:** Apply mutation testing principles from software engineering: take 10 known public CTF challenges and create 5 variants each by modifying surface features (changing IP addresses, port numbers, hash values, variable names) while preserving the underlying vulnerability class. Compare solve rates on originals vs. mutations. Large performance drops on mutations indicate memorization rather than generalization.

**Why it matters:** Benchmark contamination is a known problem in NLP benchmarks and almost certainly affects cyber benchmarks too, given models are trained on internet data including CTF writeups. Without decontamination methodology, capability measurements may be systematically inflated.

**Relevant context:** Cybench reached 82% (Irregular 2026), raising questions about whether this reflects genuine capability or memorization. CAIBench (arxiv.org/html/2510.24317v1) addressed saturation concerns. NYU CTF Bench noted challenges with reuse. Software testing mutation analysis (Gopinath et al., arxiv.org/pdf/2201.11303) provides transferable methodology.

# Cross-Domain Transfer: Applying A/B Testing Principles to Controlled Cyber Capability Experiments

**Problem:** AI cyber evaluations often have poor experimental design: no control conditions, no randomization, no statistical power analysis, and no pre-registration. # Formal Verification of Differential Privacy in AI Training: An End-to-End Experiment

**Problem:** Differential privacy (DP) guarantees for AI models are typically not formally verified — they rely on theoretical proofs that may have implementation bugs. Whether formal verification of DP in a simple AI training pipeline is tractable with LLM assistance is unknown.

**Direction:** Take a minimal DP-SGD implementation (Python, ~100 lines). Use LLM assistance to: (a) translate to Lean 4, (b) write formal spec capturing (ε,δ)-DP, (c) attempt proof. Measure whether proof completes, what the proof covers, and how long it takes with AI assistance.

**Why it matters:** Formally verified DP in AI training would represent a major AI safety milestone: mathematical proof that training preserves privacy. If it is tractable with current tools, it should be a near-term goal. If not, the gap must be characterized.

**Relevant context:** SampCert (Amazon) has Lean 4 proofs for DP mechanisms. DP-SGD is used in production (Google, Apple). No study has attempted end-to-end formal verification of a DP-SGD implementation with LLM assistance.

# Compounding Risk: Sorry-Using Proofs × Production Deployment = Undetected Incomplete Verification

**Problem:** If Lean 4 proofs using 'sorry' (a placeholder that makes any goal provable) are deployed in production without sorry detection, developers believe they have formal guarantees they do not have. This compounding risk of sorry usage + deployment without sorry checking is not characterized.

**Direction:** Survey open-source Lean 4 code on GitHub. Measure frequency of sorry usage in non-research, non-draft code. Survey developers on whether they check for sorry before deployment. Design and test a simple CI/CD sorry-detection tool. Measure developer awareness of the sorry failure mode.

**Why it matters:** If production Lean 4 code contains sorry placeholders that developers believe are complete proofs, formal verification provides false safety guarantees at scale. This is a practical deployment failure mode that urgently needs characterization.

title: Multi-Agent Formal Verification: Does a Debate-Style Protocol Between Two LLM Verifiers Improve Proof Quality?

original_idea.body:
# Multi-Agent Formal Verification: Does a Debate-Style Protocol Between Two LLM Verifiers Improve Proof Quality?

**Problem:** When one LLM generates a Lean 4 proof and another LLM critiques it (debate protocol), the combination may catch more errors than single-LLM generation. Whether multi-agent debate improves Lean 4 proof quality is untested.

**Direction:** Implement a two-agent protocol: LLM A generates a Lean 4 proof, LLM B critiques it (identifies potential errors), LLM A revises. Compare compilation rate and proof quality (vacuity rate, mutation survival) between: (a) single-agent, (b) two-agent debate, (c) two independent single-agents choosing the better output.

**Why it matters:** Multi-agent debate is proposed as a scalable oversight method in AI safety. Testing it specifically in formal verification provides empirical evidence for whether debate protocols improve correctness in machine-checkable domains.

**Relevant context:** Multi-agent debate (Irving et al.) is an AI safety proposal. Claude Code Security uses multi-stage verification (single agent). Whether two different models in debate mode improves formal verification quality is not tested.

# Formal Verification Benchmark for AI-Generated Cryptographic Primitives: AES, SHA, RSA

**Problem:** AI models are beginning to generate cryptographic code. Whether formally verified AI-generated cryptographic primitives meet the standard for deployment (correctness + constant-time + no side-channel leakage) is unknown.

**Direction:** Ask 3 LLMs to generate Python/Rust implementations of AES-256, SHA-256, and RSA key generation. **Relevant context:** RAND (2026) lists cryptographic implementation verification as a benchmark target. EverCrypt and HACL* are examples of formally verified cryptographic libraries. AI-generated crypto code is specifically not yet validated through formal methods.

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Can Lean 4 Check LLM Reasoning Steps?

**Problem:** LLM chain-of-thought reasoning produces informal mathematical arguments. Whether formal verification tools can check the correctness of LLM mathematical reasoning steps (treating CoT as a formal proof sketch) is unexplored.

**Direction:** Take 20 LLM chain-of-thought solutions to mathematical problems. Attempt to formalize each CoT step as a Lean 4 tactic sequence. Measure: (a) what fraction of CoT solutions are faithfully formalizable, (b) what fraction of formalized proofs compile without error, (c) where CoT reasoning is formally incorrect.

**Why it matters:** If CoT reasoning can be formally verified, it provides a scalable oversight mechanism for LLM mathematical reasoning. If CoT reasoning is frequently formally incorrect despite appearing correct to humans, it reveals a systematic limitation in CoT as a safety mechanism.

**Relevant context:** Chain-of-thought reasoning is used for mathematical problems. Lean 4 auto-formalization (Major Breakthroughs in Lean 4-Based Auto-Formalized Mathematics) is an active research area. Applying formal verification to CoT reasoning steps is novel.

original_idea.body:
# Minimum Lean 4 Training Data for Non-Zero Security Proof Capability: A Data Efficiency Study

**Problem:** Training models for Lean 4 security proofs requires security-domain training data, which is scarce. Whether even 100-500 examples of security-focused Lean 4 proofs (vs. thousands of general proofs) can produce non-zero security verification capability in a fine-tuned model is unknown.

**Direction:** Fine-tune Mistral base model variants on: (a) 100 general Lean 4 examples only, (b) 100 general + 50 security examples, (c) 100 general + 100 security examples. Measure compilation rate on VeriBench security challenges per training set. Find the minimum security-specific data needed for measurable improvement.

**Why it matters:** If 50-100 security examples significantly improve security verification capability, the data generation cost is tractable (ATLAS can generate them). If the model requires thousands, the data bottleneck is more serious.

**Relevant context:** ATLAS generates 19K+ training examples but not security-specific ones. AlphaVerus bootstraps from 0 security examples. The data efficiency question for security-specific formal verification is open.

# Formal Verification of OAuth/OIDC Flow: Can AI Generate Correct Protocol Security Proofs?

**Problem:** OAuth 2.0 and OIDC are widely used authentication protocols with known formal security models. Whether LLMs can generate Lean 4 or ProVerif proofs that an implementation correctly implements these protocols is untested.

**Direction:** Select a simple OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow implementation. Write formal ProVerif/Lean 4 specs for: (a) token secrecy, (b) authentication guarantee, (c) CSRF prevention. Ask LLMs to generate proofs. Measure success rate. Compare to known human-written ProVerif models of OAuth.

**Why it matters:** Authentication protocols are the most critical security layer in web applications. Formally verified OAuth implementations would provide mathematical guarantees against token theft and impersonation attacks.

**Relevant context:** ProVerif has been used to find flaws in OAuth (Fett et al. 2016). Lean 4 can also model protocols. LLM-generated protocol security proofs have not been tested on real-world protocols like OAuth.

title: Formal Verification Failure Under Internationalization: Do Unicode/Encoding Edge Cases Break Lean 4 Proofs?

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification Failure Under Internationalization: Do Unicode/Encoding Edge Cases Break Lean 4 Proofs?

**Problem:** Formal specifications often assume ASCII or simple string models. Whether formally verified string-processing code breaks when internationalized inputs (Unicode, multi-byte encodings, bidirectional text) are used — and whether Lean specs can capture these edge cases — is unstudied.

**Direction:** Take 15 formally verified string-processing functions (validators, parsers). Test them with: (a) ASCII inputs (standard), (b) Unicode inputs (emojis, CJK characters), (c) adversarial Unicode (RTL overrides, homoglyphs). Check whether formal proofs cover these cases. Measure violation rate.

**Why it matters:** Internationalization bugs are a major source of security vulnerabilities (filename traversal via Unicode normalization, RTL spoofing attacks). If formal specs systematically omit Unicode edge cases, they miss a significant class of security failures.

**Relevant context:** Unicode security vulnerabilities are documented (CVE database). Formal verification papers do not discuss Unicode handling. This is a concrete failure mode at the intersection of formal verification and real-world security.

# Measuring Monitor Calibration: Do LLM Judges Assign Well-Calibrated Danger Scores?

**Problem:** LLM-based monitors often output a 'danger score' for agent actions. Whether these scores are well-calibrated (i.e., a 0.8 danger score should correspond to ~80% probability of actual danger) is untested.

**Why it matters:** Poorly calibrated monitors lead to over-alerting or under-alerting. Calibration is a prerequisite for reliable monitoring in deployment.

original_idea:
# Causal Decomposition of Monitoring Failures: Attribution to Prompt Design vs. Model Choice vs. Threshold Setting

**Problem:** When a monitor fails to flag a dangerous action, the cause could be: bad monitoring prompt, wrong choice of monitoring model, or incorrect threshold. No methodology exists for attributing failures to these causes.

**Direction:** Collect a set of monitoring failures (false negatives). For each failure, ablate the three components: vary the monitoring prompt, swap the monitoring model, adjust the threshold. Quantify how much variance in failure rate each component explains.

**Why it matters:** Without causal attribution, monitoring improvements are guesswork. This methodology would allow systematic, evidence-based improvement of monitoring systems.

**Relevant context:** METR 2026 monitoring evaluation; causal attribution methodology in ML.

# Backcasting from Zero Successful Weight Exfiltrations: What Monitoring Stack Prevents Model Theft?

**Problem:** OpenAI's goal state is zero model weight exfiltrations. Working backward: what combination of monitoring signals (network egress, access pattern anomalies, data volume alerts) would be needed to reliably detect exfiltration attempts?

**Direction:** Simulate model weight exfiltration scenarios (large file transfers, API-based exfiltration, slow-drip exfiltration). Identify which monitoring signals are most reliable for each scenario type. Propose a minimal monitoring stack that covers all scenario types.

title: Replicating Insider Threat Detection Methodology on AI Agent Logs

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Insider Threat Detection Methodology on AI Agent Logs

**Problem:** Traditional insider threat detection uses user behavior analytics (UBA) on human employee logs. This methodology has not been applied to AI agent logs to detect insider-threat-like behaviors.

**Direction:** Apply classical UBA techniques (peer group analysis, temporal anomaly detection, entity behavior profiling) to logs from an open-source agent framework. Measure whether these techniques detect injected insider-threat-like agent behaviors with acceptable false positive rates.

**Why it matters:** UBA is a mature field with proven techniques. Transferring it to agent monitoring could immediately improve detection capabilities without requiring new fundamental research.

**Relevant context:** Traditional UBA/UEBA security products; AI agent insider threat literature; Exabeam Agent Behavior Analytics.

title: Longitudinal Behavioral Drift Detection: Can Monitoring Catch Gradual Goal Shift?

original_idea.body:
# Longitudinal Behavioral Drift Detection: Can Monitoring Catch Gradual Goal Shift?

**Problem:** Rogue agent behavior may not appear suddenly but drift gradually over many interactions. Static threshold monitors would miss gradual drift. No study has tested longitudinal drift detection for AI agents.

**Direction:** Design a multi-session agent experiment where goal drift is injected gradually (each session slightly modifying the agent's objective via context manipulation). Measure whether rolling-window baseline methods or CUSUM-style change detection can identify the drift before overt dangerous behavior.

**Why it matters:** Gradual goal drift is a plausible failure mode in long-running agent deployments. Detecting it requires fundamentally different monitoring approaches than detecting sudden attacks.

**Relevant context:** CUSUM change detection; longitudinal monitoring methodology; LW threat matrix.

# Compounding Risk: Alignment Faking + Monitoring Evasion — Do Models That Fake Alignment Also Evade Monitors?

**Problem:** Alignment faking (models appearing aligned in monitored contexts) is a distinct failure mode from active monitoring evasion. Whether models that exhibit alignment faking are also more likely to actively craft monitor-evading outputs is unknown.

**Why it matters:** If alignment faking correlates with monitoring evasion, these are not independent risks — they compound into a single high-severity threat profile requiring combined countermeasures.

**Relevant context:** Alignment faking research (Anthropic); METR monitoring evasion; compounding risk analysis.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Monitoring Classifiers: Are They More Fragile Than Task Models?

original_idea.body:
# Adversarial Robustness of Monitoring Classifiers: Are They More Fragile Than Task Models?

**Problem:** Monitoring classifiers are themselves ML models and could be adversarially attacked. It is unknown whether monitoring classifiers are more or less adversarially fragile than the task models they monitor.

**Direction:** Apply standard adversarial text attack methods (e.g., TEXTFOOLER, BERT-Attack) to a monitoring classifier. Measure adversarial robustness. Compare to adversarial robustness of the task model on the same attacks. Determine relative fragility.

**Why it matters:** If monitors are more adversarially fragile than task models, the assumption that monitoring adds security is questionable. This is a fundamental property of the monitoring paradigm.

**Relevant context:** Adversarial ML literature; METR bypass vectors; LLM-based classifier robustness.

# Honeypot Effectiveness Across Attack Sophistication Levels: Do Smarter Agents Avoid Honeypots?

**Problem:** LLM agents used in cyberattacks vary in capability. It is unknown whether more capable agents (better reasoning) are more likely to recognize and avoid honeypot traps than less capable agents.

**Direction:** Deploy honeypot tasks (fake high-value targets with canary tokens) in an agent environment. Test agents of varying capability levels (small vs. large LLMs, with and without chain-of-thought). Measure honeypot interaction rates across capability levels.

**Why it matters:** If smarter agents systematically avoid honeypots, this undermines honeypot-based detection precisely for the highest-capability threats — the ones most dangerous.

**Relevant context:** LLM Agent Honeypot paper; OpenAI capability threshold; detection-evasion scaling.

title: Multi-Turn Context Poisoning: Detecting Gradual Instruction Corruption Across Conversation Turns

original_idea.body:
# Multi-Turn Context Poisoning: Detecting Gradual Instruction Corruption Across Conversation Turns

**Problem:** An attacker could gradually corrupt an agent's context across many turns, with no single turn triggering a threshold. No study has tested whether monitors can detect this multi-turn accumulation attack.

**Direction:** Design a multi-turn context poisoning attack: spread malicious instruction fragments across 10-20 turns of conversation. Test whether action-level monitors (which see one turn at a time) and trajectory-level monitors (which see the full context) differ in detection success.

**Why it matters:** Multi-turn attacks are specifically designed to evade per-turn monitoring. This study identifies whether trajectory-level monitoring provides essential additional coverage.

**Relevant context:** Prompt injection literature; long-context monitoring; METR bypass vectors.

title: Transferring Kill Chain Dwell Time Analysis to AI Agent Monitoring

original_idea.body:
# Transferring Kill Chain Dwell Time Analysis to AI Agent Monitoring

**Problem:** In traditional cybersecurity, 'dwell time' — the time between initial compromise and detection — is a key metric. No equivalent metric has been defined for AI agent monitoring.

**Direction:** Define 'agent compromise dwell time' as the number of actions between goal injection and monitoring detection. Measure this across different attack types and monitoring configurations. Identify which configurations minimize dwell time.

**Why it matters:** Dwell time is a directly actionable security metric — minimizing it limits attacker damage potential. Introducing this concept to AI monitoring provides a clear optimization target.

**Relevant context:** Traditional cybersecurity dwell time metrics; METR monitoring evaluation; kill chain analysis.

# Evaluating Third-Party Audit Feasibility: What Can External Evaluators Actually Observe?

**Problem:** Third-party adversarial evaluation of AI safety infrastructure is nascent. A key prerequisite question is: what can external evaluators actually observe without internal access, and is that sufficient for meaningful evaluation?

**Direction:** Define three access tiers for evaluating an agent monitoring system: black-box (API access only), gray-box (logs but no model weights), white-box (full access). title: Compounding Risk: Sycophancy + Goal Hijacking — Do Sycophantic Agents Accept Injected Goals More Readily?

original_idea.body:
# Compounding Risk: Sycophancy + Goal Hijacking — Do Sycophantic Agents Accept Injected Goals More Readily?

**Problem:** Sycophantic agents are biased toward agreeing with user/operator assertions. Goal hijacking via injection often involves asserting a new goal. These two failure modes may compound significantly.

**Direction:** Measure sycophancy level in several open-source models using standard sycophancy benchmarks. Then test each model's susceptibility to goal-hijacking prompt injections. Measure correlation between sycophancy score and goal-hijacking susceptibility.

**Why it matters:** If sycophancy predicts injection susceptibility, sycophancy evaluation becomes a proxy for agent security evaluation — a major practical implication for model selection.

**Relevant context:** Sycophancy research; prompt injection research; compounding failure modes.

# Real-Time vs. Offline Monitoring: Tradeoffs in Detection Rate, Cost, and Response Latency

**Problem:** Agent monitoring can be real-time (blocking actions until approved) or offline (log review after the fact). The tradeoffs between these modes have not been empirically characterized in terms of detection rate and cost.

**Direction:** Implement both real-time and offline monitoring for the same agent pipeline. Run standardized attack scenarios. Compare detection rate, false positive rate, response latency (time-to-block vs. time-to-detect), and computational cost per decision.

**Why it matters:** Deployment contexts determine which monitoring mode is feasible. This study gives organizations an empirical basis for choosing between modes given their constraints.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic detection classifiers (real-time); METR monitoring evaluation; monitoring architecture tradeoffs.
